newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss economy to recover, but franc decides - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Swiss economy to recover, but franc decides - OECD.

text.p: The Swiss economy is set to recover in the next few years after lengthy stagnation provided the Swiss franc does not surge again, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said on Thursday.

The Paris-based OECD expects Switzerland's gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by 0.8 percent in 1997 and 2.0 percent in 1998, after a likely 0.3 percent fall in 1996. The economy grew by a meagre 0.1 percent in 1995.

The projections in the OECD's half-yearly report are slightly more upbeat than those of the Swiss government's Commission for Economic Policy which recently forecast a 0.75 percent fall in 1996 GDP and 0.5 percent expansion in 1997.
The Swiss National Bank (SNB) also expects 0.5 percent growth in 1997.

The OECD and Swiss government agree Switzerland's recovery in 1997 should be lead by its export sector, which saw its competitiveness hammered by a 19 percent nominal appreciation in the franc in the past four years.
Exports should expand 3.5 percent in 1997 and 5.0 percent in 1998 following 1996's rise of only 1.8 percent, the OECD said.

The SNB's policy of guiding the franc lower this year is expected to remain successful with the harsh effects of the franc's previous rise petering out. The mark has surged to over 85 Swiss centimes from around 80.50 in January.
The SNB has said it will continue its generous monetary policy into 1997 and not push up interest rates because of the weak economy and uncertainty about Europe's single currency.
However, the OECD cautioned that events in foreign exchange markets could upset its projections.

"The Swiss economy's international competitiveness could be weakened further if concerns of international investors about the future strength of the euro after European Monetary Union takes place continued to raise demand for Swiss francs," the OECD said.

The Swiss government's efforts to cut spending will remain a drag on the economy, but the gradual economic recovery should help reverse record-high unemployment, thus allowing a modest acceleration in private consumption.
The unemployment rate should rise to 4.8 percent in 1997 from 1996's 4.6 percent, but then ease to 4.5 percent in 1998.
Inflation is expected to remain low due to the large output gap in industry despite the diminishing price-dampening effects of the franc's rise, the OECD said.
Consumer prices are forecast to rise 1.2 percent in 1997 and 1.4 percent in 1998 after 0.7 percent in 1996.
